lessons.name: Advanced Machine Intelligence (AMI)
lessons.summary: AMI is an AI research lab developing world models that predict the consequences of actions from real-world sensor data.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

AMI is an AI research lab developing world models that predict the consequences of actions from real-world sensor data.

![AMI’s official geometric logo](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-ami.webp)
*AMI’s official geometric logo. Source: [Publisher](https://amilabs.xyz/updates), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **World models** predict how a situation might change; AMI aims to predict useful internal representations rather than every future camera pixel.
- **Action-conditioned prediction** means including a proposed action as input, so an agent can compare possible futures before choosing a move.
- **The organization spans four cities:** Paris, New York, Montreal and Singapore. Its March 2026 launch announcement describes a world-model research program, not a robot catalogue.

> **Key idea:** Predicting useful consequences is different from generating a visually convincing video.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Think of a dry-run API:** proposed actions go in; predicted consequences come out. Unlike a deterministic program, the learned predictor can be wrong.
- **Connect V-JEPA 2 / JEPA world models** to the map project World-model planning on the SO-101 as a learning direction, not an advertised AMI product.
- **A worked thought experiment:** compare “move the gripper left” with “close it now”; ask which prediction would help decide whether an object gets grasped.

## How to engage

1. **Watch LeCun explain the approach**, then distinguish research goals from demonstrated capabilities in your notes.
2. **Read AMI’s official updates** before attributing software, hardware or results to the company.
3. **Use its public contact channel** for a focused technical question; bring a small experiment and explicitly state what failed.

lessons.name: AIST
lessons.summary: AIST is Japan’s National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, whose humanoid research includes robots for heavy physical work.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

AIST is Japan’s National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology, whose humanoid research includes robots for heavy physical work.

![AIST’s HRP-5P humanoid standing and carrying a large board](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-aist.webp)
*AIST’s HRP-5P humanoid standing and carrying a large board. Source: [Publisher](https://www.aist.go.jp/aist_e/list/latest_research/2018/20181116/en20181116.html), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **HRP-5P is a research prototype:** the 2018 report describes a 182-centimetre, 101-kilogram humanoid, not a consumer robot available for a student desk.
- **A concrete demonstration:** it maps a mock construction site, lifts a gypsum board, carries it to a wall, picks up a screwdriver and fastens it.
- **Whole-body control** coordinates legs, torso and arms so manipulating a large object does not become a separate problem from staying upright.

> **Key idea:** A useful humanoid demonstration integrates perception, movement and tool use, rather than showcasing walking alone.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **HRP-5P** is the related map node: use its board-installation sequence to identify the responsibilities a complete robot system must connect.
- **Think continuous integration for robots:** AIST describes regression monitoring in the Choreonoid simulator for roughly 250,000 lines of robot-intelligence software.
- **Learn the integration lesson**, not the hardware scale: a tabletop project can also test perception, planning and execution separately before combining them.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the official demonstration** and write down where sensing ends and physical action begins.
2. **Read the dated research report**, separating the demonstrated installation from its proposed future construction applications.
3. **Follow AIST’s public research releases** and prepare one specific question about testing or failure recovery rather than requesting access to a humanoid.

lessons.name: Ampère
lessons.summary: Ampère is a Lyon-area research laboratory whose robotics work includes control systems and physical simulators for practising medical gestures.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Ampère is a Lyon-area research laboratory whose robotics work includes control systems and physical simulators for practising medical gestures.

![Published BirthSIM visualization showing forceps and a model pelvis from several viewpoints](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-ampere.webp)
*Published BirthSIM visualization showing forceps and a model pelvis from several viewpoints. Source: [Publisher](https://hal.science/hal-00399361/document), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **BirthSIM is a concrete example:** this childbirth-training simulator combines a model pelvis, a model baby’s head, sensors and a computer-controlled pneumatic mechanism.
- **Pneumatic actuation** uses compressed air to produce movement and resistance. The simulator reproduces physical effort, not just images on a screen.
- **Haptics means touch feedback:** the trainee feels resistance while the system records movement and forces for analysis.

> **Key idea:** A medical simulator must reproduce the physical interaction being learned, not merely display an animation.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Think of a physical test harness:** an instructor’s reference gesture provides a target; recorded trainee movements make differences visible and measurable.
- **Worked example:** track forceps placement, display their path inside the model pelvis, then compare that path with the reference rather than judging appearance alone.
- **Broaden our robotics interests:** Ampère’s work connects software to sensing, control and medical training, beyond the usual tabletop pick-and-place demonstration.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the BirthSIM demonstration** and identify which parts are mechanical models and which parts are computer visualization.
2. **Read the original team’s paper** for the instrumented setup; treat it as a historical research design, not a current equipment listing.
3. **Use public laboratory channels** to ask a focused educational question about measurement or touch feedback; do not propose testing student prototypes on patients.

lessons.name: BAAI (Beijing Academy of Artificial Intelligence)
lessons.summary: BAAI develops robot-oriented AI models, including RoboBrain, that connect visual observations and language instructions to reasoning about physical tasks.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

BAAI develops robot-oriented AI models, including RoboBrain, that connect visual observations and language instructions to reasoning about physical tasks.

![RoboBrain 2.0 published visualization of spatial and temporal reasoning examples](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-baai.webp)
*RoboBrain 2.0 published visualization of spatial and temporal reasoning examples. Source: [Publisher](https://superrobobrain.github.io/robobrainv2/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **RoboBrain 2.0** combines a vision encoder, which converts pictures into features, with a language model that processes instructions and generates structured answers.
- **Spatial reasoning** concerns where objects are and how they relate; temporal reasoning concerns what happens over time or which step comes next.
- **The work is inspectable:** BAAI publishes project demonstrations, model checkpoints and a technical report. The current project homepage also presents RoboBrain 2.5.

> **Key idea:** Reasoning about an action is one part of a robot system; it does not replace the controller moving its motors.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Use a software analogy:** treat the model as a planning service with typed inputs and outputs, not as a function guaranteed to be correct.
- **Worked example:** request the location of an object from an image, inspect the predicted coordinates, then check them against the visible target before considering execution.
- **Follow the RoboBrain 2.0 map node** to study the interface between visual understanding and robot planning, while keeping version-specific results separate.

## How to engage

1. **Watch an official project-linked demo** and distinguish visible robot behavior from the model output illustrated alongside it.
2. **Read the model card’s access conditions** before downloading weights; a public page does not imply unrestricted file access.
3. **Use the repository issue tracker** with the exact checkpoint, input image and unexpected output when reporting a reproducible problem.

lessons.name: Beijing Innovation Center of Humanoid Robotics (X-Humanoid)
lessons.summary: X-Humanoid is a Beijing robotics center developing humanoid platforms, embodied-AI software and datasets for learning physical tasks.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

X-Humanoid is a Beijing robotics center developing humanoid platforms, embodied-AI software and datasets for learning physical tasks.

![X-Humanoid’s published industrial parts-sorting robot demonstration image](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-x-humanoid.webp)
*X-Humanoid’s published industrial parts-sorting robot demonstration image. Source: [Publisher](https://x-humanoid.com), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Established in November 2023**, the center is based in Beijing’s Yizhuang area. Its public projects connect robot bodies, software and training data.
- **TianGong 3.0** is a related hardware node; RoboMIND (dataset) is a related data node. These are different outputs of the same ecosystem.
- **A concrete data example:** the original RoboMIND release describes 107,000 real-world demonstrations across four robot types, with camera observations, robot states and language descriptions.

> **Key idea:** Sharing a robot design and sharing demonstrations solve different barriers to reproducing robotics research.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Think of a dataset as an API contract:** consistent fields and recording rules help software consume experiments collected on different robot bodies.
- **Embodiment means physical form:** an arm and a humanoid have different joints and capabilities, even when both demonstrations say “pick up the object”.
- **Worked example:** inspect a RoboMIND task description, its camera views and joint-state fields together; ask what a student arm would need to reproduce that task.

## How to engage

1. **Watch Tiangong footage** to understand the hardware, without mistaking a running demonstration for evidence of manipulation performance.
2. **Read RoboMIND’s collection protocol** and distinguish the original release from the newer V2.0 listing.
3. **Use Open-X-Humanoid’s public community** to report dataset or toolchain issues with a sample identifier and reproducible steps.

lessons.name: Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research (BAIR)
lessons.summary: BAIR is UC Berkeley’s artificial-intelligence research community, including teams that teach robots physical skills through demonstrations and reinforcement learning.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

BAIR is UC Berkeley’s artificial-intelligence research community, including teams that teach robots physical skills through demonstrations and reinforcement learning.

![Berkeley HIL-SERL’s published system overview linking human correction, robot experience and learning](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-bair.webp)
*Berkeley HIL-SERL’s published system overview linking human correction, robot experience and learning. Source: [Publisher](https://hil-serl.github.io/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **HIL-SERL** is a concrete Berkeley example: it learns manipulation skills using demonstrations, robot experience and corrections supplied by a human operator.
- **Reinforcement learning** improves a policy through feedback from attempted actions; a policy is the function choosing what the robot should do next.
- **A success classifier** is trained from successful and unsuccessful examples. Its yes/no prediction supplies a reward signal during learning.

> **Key idea:** Helpful human corrections and a usable success signal can make real-robot learning much more practical.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Think interactive debugging:** rather than only reviewing a final failure, an operator corrects behavior during training, adding useful experience for subsequent updates.
- **A concrete worked example:** follow the repository’s RAM-insertion task and identify demonstration collection, success detection, policy training and evaluation as separate responsibilities.
- **Learn system design from HIL-SERL**, not just an algorithm name: its actor runs robot interactions while a separate learner updates and synchronizes the policy.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the project introduction** and choose one manipulation task to understand before opening the code.
2. **Read the hardware requirements** before attempting reproduction; a Franka-oriented setup is not a drop-in driver for an arbitrary student arm.
3. **Use public code and project channels** for reproducibility questions; include task configuration, hardware, software version and a minimal failure case.

lessons.name: BFH HuCE Robotics Laboratory
lessons.summary: BFH’s HuCE Robotics Laboratory develops collaborative, industrial and mobile robotics, with applications in manufacturing and medicine.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

BFH’s HuCE Robotics Laboratory develops collaborative, industrial and mobile robotics, with applications in manufacturing and medicine.

![Robot equipment in BFH’s HuCE Robotics Laboratory](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-bfh.webp)
*Robot equipment in BFH’s HuCE Robotics Laboratory. Source: [Publisher](https://www.bfh.ch/en/research/research-areas/roboticslab/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Collaborative robotics** studies robots working with people in shared workspaces. BFH’s demonstrations include obstacle avoidance, moving targets and learning from demonstrations.
- **A concrete behavior:** the obstacle-avoidance system detects a person and changes its planned path; if it cannot find a path, the robot stops.
- **The equipment list includes P-Rob**, Franka Emika Panda, UR3 and Meca500. P-Rob is the related map node, not a robot invented by BFH.

> **Key idea:** Collaboration is a property of the whole interaction system, not simply a label attached to a robot arm.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Think goal-based programming:** specify where an object should end up, while a planner computes a movement path that can change when the environment changes.
- **Worked example:** compare a fixed recorded path with BFH’s moving-target demonstration; note when reaching the goal requires changing intermediate movements.
- **Learn applied integration:** image processing, control and mechanical design meet in the lab’s industrial and medical projects, beyond training an AI model in isolation.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the laboratory’s demonstrations** and separate obstacle avoidance from learning a task through examples.
2. **Read the facilities and expertise sections** to choose a precise topic, such as goal-based trajectories or human-presence detection.
3. **Ask through public laboratory contacts** about an educational demonstration or visit; the page explicitly lists practical visits, but access still needs agreement.

lessons.name: EPFL Biorobotics Laboratory (BioRob)
lessons.summary: EPFL’s BioRob laboratory uses animal-inspired robots and simulations to understand movement and develop locomotion controllers.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EPFL’s BioRob laboratory uses animal-inspired robots and simulations to understand movement and develop locomotion controllers.

![BioRob’s salamander-shaped Pleurobot seen from above](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-biorob.webp)
*BioRob’s salamander-shaped Pleurobot seen from above. Source: [Publisher](https://www.epfl.ch/labs/biorob/research/amphibious/pleurobot/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Biology informs engineering:** the laboratory studies how nervous systems and bodies produce movement, then tests ideas in simulations and physical robots.
- **Pleurobot** reproduces salamander movements using a body design informed by three-dimensional X-ray recordings; its 27 controllable joints make the comparison concrete.
- **Central pattern generators** are rhythm-producing controller models. BioRob investigates how these patterns coordinate limbs and body waves for walking and swimming.

> **Key idea:** A robot can be an experiment for understanding animal movement, not only a machine built to complete a useful task.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Think of a physics-backed unit test:** a proposed movement controller must work with a real body, rather than merely produce plausible animation.
- **Worked reading exercise:** compare Pleurobot walking and swimming; list which body parts change rhythm and which movements the mechanical design permits.
- **Follow the map’s Salamandra robotica and AmphiBot** to compare related amphibious platforms without assuming that they share identical joints or controllers.

## How to engage

1. **Watch Ijspeert’s public talk** before reading the Pleurobot design page; identify the question each robot helps the researchers investigate.
2. **Compare the amphibious projects** and pick one movement pattern to reproduce in a small software simulation, not an unsupervised hardware build.
3. **Use BioRob’s public research and teaching pages** to formulate a specific question about reproducing a movement experiment.

lessons.name: EPFL Reconfigurable Robotics Lab (RRL)
lessons.summary: EPFL’s Reconfigurable Robotics Lab develops folding, shape-changing and soft robots whose physical structure contributes to their capabilities.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EPFL’s Reconfigurable Robotics Lab develops folding, shape-changing and soft robots whose physical structure contributes to their capabilities.

![Folded Tribot robots resting in a human palm](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-rrl.webp)
*Folded Tribot robots resting in a human palm. Source: [Publisher](https://www.epfl.ch/labs/rrl/research-2/research-origami/tribot/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Reconfiguration** means changing physical arrangement, not merely loading different software. The lab combines mechanical design, fabrication, actuation and control.
- **Tribot is a concrete example:** its published battery-powered prototype weighs ten grams and switches between walking, crawling and several kinds of jumping.
- **Mori3 uses triangular modules:** units connect and rearrange into articulated structures. Its 2023 report presents space applications as a motivation, not a completed deployment.

> **Key idea:** Changing the body can change what a controller is able to accomplish.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Think reusable software components, with physical connectors:** modules must exchange information, but also support loads and move without blocking one another.
- **Worked comparison:** contrast Tribot’s crawling and jumping. Mark what changes in the mechanism and what the controller must select.
- **Use EPFL Robotics Center** as the related map entry for finding neighboring expertise; RRL itself is the specialist in reconfigurable robot design.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the official Tribot demonstration** and separate a single robot’s capabilities from behavior that requires coordination between several robots.
2. **Read the fabrication explanation** before assuming a folded robot is simply a paper model with a motor attached.
3. **Follow public lab publications and contacts** with a focused simulation or design question; share drawings or code rather than requesting unspecified collaboration.

lessons.name: ETH Zurich Institute for Dynamic Systems and Control (IDSC)
lessons.summary: ETH Zurich’s IDSC studies dynamic systems and control, including how robots can improve repeated movements by learning from previous attempts.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

ETH Zurich’s IDSC studies dynamic systems and control, including how robots can improve repeated movements by learning from previous attempts.

![IDSC’s published illustration for its iterative-learning research](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-idsc.webp)
*IDSC’s published illustration for its iterative-learning research. Source: [Publisher](https://idsc.ethz.ch/research-dandrea/research-projects/archive/iterative-learning.html), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Control** chooses inputs that make a physical system behave as intended; IDSC’s archived robotics work includes repeated high-speed quadrocopter maneuvers.
- **Iterative learning** uses the difference between a desired movement and the measured result to adjust the command for the next attempt.
- **A historical worked example:** the archive describes learning a triple flip over about 40 trials, reaching a turn rate of 1,600 degrees per second.

> **Key idea:** Learning between attempts and correcting errors during an attempt are distinct jobs that can support each other.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **Think benchmark-driven optimization:** run the same task, log the error, change the input and repeat; comparisons require a consistent task.
- **Connect Feedback control & PID** to this example: reacting to an error now differs from improving a feedforward command for the next repetition.
- **Read the archive as history**, not a claim about current equipment access or a ready-made flight recipe for student hardware.

## How to engage

1. **Watch the researcher’s flip demonstration**, then identify what was repeated and what counted as a successful final movement.
2. **Recreate the learning idea in simulation:** compare the endpoint error of a repeated movement before and after a command update.
3. **Use public IDSC research pages** to ask a narrow methodological question; avoid reproducing aggressive flight near people.

lessons.name: EPFL Computational Robot Design & Fabrication Lab (CREATE)
lessons.summary: EPFL CREATE designs robot bodies and experiments, including soft grippers trained with an instrumented imitation raspberry.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EPFL CREATE designs robot bodies and experiments, including soft grippers trained with an instrumented imitation raspberry.

![CREATE raspberry-harvesting experiment](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-create.webp)
*CREATE raspberry-harvesting experiment. Source: [Publisher](https://actu.epfl.ch/news/silicone-raspberry-used-to-train-harvesting-robo-3), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Robot design:** CREATE studies how a robot’s body affects its abilities, combining fabrication, sensing, experiments, and computation.
- **Soft robotics** uses flexible structures rather than only rigid links; CREATE explores soft arms, tactile hands, and robots interacting with fluids.
- **Concrete example:** its silicone raspberry contains a fluid-filled sensor; two magnets reproduce attachment to the plant so a gripper can practise detaching it.
- **Software analogy:** this physical twin is a reusable test fixture, giving a controller feedback before experiments with fragile real fruit.

> **Key idea:** A better training environment can teach a controller what its cameras cannot see: how hard it is squeezing.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For our lab:** agricultural manipulation connects vision and learning to contact forces, where a successful grasp must not destroy the object.
- **Related map:** EPFL Soft Transducers Laboratory (LMTS) offers a complementary view of the flexible components that make soft machines work.

## How to engage

1. **Watch** the harvesting demonstration and identify approach, grasp, pull, and release.
2. **Read** the raspberry article; distinguish the demonstrated prototype from planned field work.
3. **Try** a software-only picking state machine that reduces its grip command when a simulated attachment sensor switches off.

lessons.name: EPFL Laboratory of Intelligent Systems (LIS)
lessons.summary: EPFL LIS studies intelligent, nature-inspired robots, including drones whose bodies help them move between ground and air.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EPFL LIS studies intelligent, nature-inspired robots, including drones whose bodies help them move between ground and air.

![RAVEN drone with bird-inspired legs](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-lis.webp)
*RAVEN drone with bird-inspired legs. Source: [Publisher](https://actu.epfl.ch/news/bird-inspired-drone-can-jump-for-take-off-4), CC BY SA.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Aerial robotics:** LIS designs flying machines with sensing and movement abilities for open skies, confined spaces, surfaces, and groups of robots.
- **Concrete example:** RAVEN is a 0.62-kilogram fixed-wing drone with legs that let it walk, hop, and jump into flight.
- **Mechanical design:** springs and motors imitate useful functions of bird tendons and muscles; heavier components stay close to the body.
- **Software analogy:** its movement modes resemble a state machine: walking and take-off need different commands but share the same hardware.

> **Key idea:** Autonomy depends on a body that can reach useful places, not just an algorithm that chooses where to go.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** RAVEN makes an accessible study of how physical design constrains planning and control, even before we build flying hardware.
- **Related map:** EPFL Biorobotics Laboratory (BioRob) collaborated on RAVEN; compare its animal-inspired movement research with LIS’s aerial focus.

## How to engage

1. **Watch** RAVEN walking and taking off; mark when the mode changes.
2. **Read** the official article and sketch which functions come from springs, motors, and software.
3. **Explore** the aerial-robotics publications; propose a ground-only simulation of transitions before attempting flight.

lessons.name: EPFL Learning Algorithms and Systems Laboratory (LASA)
lessons.summary: EPFL LASA teaches robots dexterous movement through human demonstrations and control methods that adapt during interaction.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EPFL LASA teaches robots dexterous movement through human demonstrations and control methods that adapt during interaction.

![LASA robot catching an object in flight](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-lasa.webp)
*LASA robot catching an object in flight. Source: [Publisher](https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lasa/catching-objects-flight/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Learning from demonstration** means using examples of human movement to teach a robot a skill rather than specifying every motion by hand.
- **Reactive control** updates movement as conditions change; LASA studies manipulation, shared control, and interaction with people.
- **Concrete example:** its catching-objects work asks a robot to meet a moving object, rather than grasping something already stationary on a table.
- **Software analogy:** a demonstration is like an example input/output test; the controller still needs to generalize beyond the exact recorded case.

> **Key idea:** A recorded movement is a starting point; robust physical interaction requires adapting that movement while it happens.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** LASA connects our machine-learning background to robot motion, where timing, contact, and disturbances matter as much as prediction accuracy.
- **Related map:** EPFL Computational Robot Design & Fabrication Lab (CREATE) complements LASA by studying the bodies and experimental setups used for manipulation.

## How to engage

1. **Watch** the catching demonstration and identify what changes between attempts.
2. **Explore** the research gallery, separating skill learning from the control that executes a skill.
3. **Try** replaying a recorded cursor path toward a moved target; compare literal replay with adapting the endpoint.

lessons.name: EPFL Soft Transducers Laboratory (LMTS)
lessons.summary: EPFL LMTS develops flexible devices that turn electrical energy into movement, pumping, or touch sensations for soft robots and wearables.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EPFL LMTS develops flexible devices that turn electrical energy into movement, pumping, or touch sensations for soft robots and wearables.

![LMTS flat swimming robot with soft fins](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-lmts.webp)
*LMTS flat swimming robot with soft fins. Source: [Publisher](https://www.epfl.ch/labs/lmts/lmts-research/elastomer_actuator/untethered-agile-flat-swimming-robot/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **A transducer** converts one kind of energy into another; an actuator produces movement, while a sensor measures a physical effect.
- **Soft components:** LMTS develops stretchable actuators, tactile displays, flexible pumps, and small robotic devices.
- **Concrete example:** its 2025 swimming robot measures 5 × 5 centimetres and carries electronics while flexible fins generate propulsion.
- **Wearable example:** its fiber pump is a roughly 2-millimetre tube with internal electrodes that move liquid electrically.
- **Software analogy:** these components are hardware interfaces: the controller sends electrical commands, but the device determines the resulting force or flow.

> **Key idea:** Choosing an actuator changes what a robot can physically do, even when its control program stays the same.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** LMTS makes the hardware beneath a robot-learning policy visible: power, flexibility, and sensing constrain the action space.
- **Related map:** compare its component research with complete soft machines at EPFL Reconfigurable Robotics Lab (RRL).

## How to engage

1. **Watch** the swimming robot; identify how fin waves replace propellers.
2. **Read** the fiber-pump explanation and trace command, liquid flow, and physical effect.
3. **Start** with published demonstrations; these electrical actuation experiments involve high voltage, not a breadboard beginner build.

lessons.name: EPFL Translational Neural Engineering Lab (TNE)
lessons.summary: EPFL TNE develops interfaces between people and technology, including sensory prostheses and methods for controlling an extra robotic limb.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EPFL TNE develops interfaces between people and technology, including sensory prostheses and methods for controlling an extra robotic limb.

![Virtual-reality experiment studying control of an extra arm](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-tne.webp)
*Virtual-reality experiment studying control of an extra arm. Source: [Publisher](https://actu.epfl.ch/news/cognitive-strategies-to-augment-the-body-with-an-6), CC-BY-SA.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Neuroengineering** connects knowledge of the nervous system with engineered devices, aiming to restore or extend useful functions.
- **Sensory feedback** returns information to the person; commanding an artificial limb and feeling its effects are different engineering problems.
- **Concrete example:** an extra-arm study used a belt measuring diaphragm movement to control a third virtual arm alongside two natural-arm interfaces.
- **Physical test:** researchers also used breathing to extend and retract a simplified robotic rod; this was not a general-purpose third hand.
- **Software analogy:** the interface maps a new input channel to an output device, but the human must learn that mapping too.

> **Key idea:** A human-robot interface succeeds only when the person can learn to control it alongside their existing actions.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** TNE offers a human-centered counterpart to autonomous manipulation: measure usability and learning, not only robot accuracy.
- **Related map:** EPFL Learning Algorithms and Systems Laboratory (LASA) provides another perspective on people teaching and interacting with robots.

## How to engage

1. **Watch** the extra-arm demonstration, distinguishing virtual and physical experiments.
2. **Read** the study article; note which participants and devices were actually tested.
3. **Prototype** a keyboard-controlled extra cursor and log interference with a normal mouse task; do not claim clinical benefit.

lessons.name: EPFL Robotics Center
lessons.summary: EPFL Robotics Center connects the university’s robotics laboratories, education, and external partners rather than building one single robot.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

EPFL Robotics Center connects the university’s robotics laboratories, education, and external partners rather than building one single robot.

![EPFL robotics laboratory tour preview](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-epfl-center.webp)
*EPFL robotics laboratory tour preview. Source: [Publisher](https://www.epfl.ch/research/domains/robotics/virtual-lab-tour/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **A connecting organization:** the center links robotics research, education, and innovation across laboratories with different specialties.
- **Different scales:** its public lab directory spans robot design, intelligent systems, learning, medical applications, and human interaction.
- **Concrete example:** the virtual tour lets you compare a BioRob locomotion laboratory video with a CREATE design-and-fabrication laboratory video.
- **Software analogy:** think of the center as a package registry: it helps locate the right specialist rather than implementing every capability itself.

> **Key idea:** Find the laboratory behind a demonstration; a university-wide robotics center is an entry point, not one homogeneous research team.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** the tour is a fast way for software students to discover physical problems beyond our first robot-learning project.
- **Related map:** compare EPFL Biorobotics Laboratory (BioRob), EPFL Laboratory of Intelligent Systems (LIS), and EPFL Learning Algorithms and Systems Laboratory (LASA).

## How to engage

1. **Watch** two contrasting lab-tour videos and list each team’s robot, input signals, and task.
2. **Use** the lab directory to find the original project and publications, rather than treating a center overview as technical documentation.
3. **Engage** through the center’s published contact or public activities with one specific technical question and a link to our demo.

lessons.name: Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute
lessons.summary: Carnegie Mellon’s Robotics Institute brings together research and education on robots that sense, plan, move, and interact with people.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

Carnegie Mellon’s Robotics Institute brings together research and education on robots that sense, plan, move, and interact with people.

![Students operating a drone at CMU’s Robotics Innovation Center](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-cmu-ri.webp)
*Students operating a drone at CMU’s Robotics Innovation Center. Source: [Publisher](https://www.ri.cmu.edu/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **A broad institute:** its research spans perception, planning, physical interaction, and robot embodiment—the choice of a robot’s body.
- **Concrete example:** the institute describes field robots for land, sea, and air, alongside healthcare systems such as assistive feeding devices.
- **Different teams:** specialized laboratories work on computer vision, human-robot interaction, learning, manipulation, and other parts of robotic systems.
- **Software analogy:** this is an engineering organization with many libraries and maintainers, not a single model or robot to download.

> **Key idea:** A robot demonstration combines several specialties; use the institute’s research map to identify which one a project actually advances.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** the public seminar recordings expose the reasoning behind research, including assumptions and failures that short highlight clips omit.
- **Related map:** compare its breadth with Berkeley Artificial Intelligence Research (BAIR), then choose one tightly scoped question rather than copying an entire platform.

## How to engage

1. **Start** with the research overview and assign a demonstration to sensing, thinking, interaction, or embodiment.
2. **Watch** a seminar’s introduction and experiment section before its mathematical details.
3. **Follow** the relevant lab’s publications and public project links; write down what hardware, data, and code a reproduction would need.

lessons.name: CESI LINEACT
lessons.summary: CESI LINEACT studies digital innovation using physical research platforms, including production systems with mobile robots and collaborative arms.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

CESI LINEACT studies digital innovation using physical research platforms, including production systems with mobile robots and collaborative arms.

![CESI LINEACT robotic research platforms](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-cesi-lineact.webp)
*CESI LINEACT robotic research platforms. Source: [Publisher](https://lineact.cesi.fr/unite-de-recherche/plateformes-technologiques/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Industrial systems:** LINEACT connects computing with production equipment, human operators, and the organization of work.
- **Concrete example:** its Rouen production platform combines an automated line, manual workstations, mobile transport robots, and robot arms.
- **A digital twin** is a digital counterpart of a physical system; LINEACT pairs its production platform with one for research and teaching.
- **Historical example:** CoRoT targeted reusable software for arms, mobile manipulators, and production supervision, including industrial and low-cost mobile platforms.
- **Software analogy:** a factory resembles a distributed application: individual robot services must coordinate with scheduling, monitoring, and people.

> **Key idea:** Automating one motion is different from integrating a robot into a production workflow that must keep running.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** these platforms connect our software skills to practical integration questions: transport, assembly, simulation, and human interfaces.
- **Related map:** compare LINEACT’s production-system perspective with CEA-List’s smart-robotics research.

## How to engage

1. **Watch** the laboratory’s collaborative virtual-reality demonstration; identify how a shared digital workspace supports production-layout decisions.
2. **Read** the platform description and draw the equipment and information flows.
3. **Use** public project pages and contacts to ask one focused integration question; access to physical facilities is not automatically public.

lessons.name: CRIStAL (Lille)
lessons.summary: CRIStAL is a Lille research center studying computer science and control, including robots that perceive, decide, and act in the physical world.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

CRIStAL is a Lille research center studying computer science and control, including robots that perceive, decide, and act in the physical world.

![Official CRIStAL research-center logo](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-cristal.webp)
*Official CRIStAL research-center logo. Source: [Publisher](https://www.cristal.univ-lille.fr/axes/robotique/), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Cyber-physical systems** combine computation with physical equipment; CRIStAL’s robotics axis connects sensors, decisions, actuators, and embedded computing.
- **Robotics platforms:** PRETIL supports experiments in robotics, intelligent transport, and mobility, including maintaining equipment researchers depend on.
- **Concrete example:** a university laboratory video explains combining a rigid robotic arm with a flexible needle for minimally invasive medical procedures.
- **Software analogy:** the controller resembles a continuously running service, but its outputs change physical motion rather than only a database.

> **Key idea:** Robotics needs perception, decisions, and action to work together; success in one module does not establish success of the whole machine.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** CRIStAL provides a French research entry point for understanding how software meets control, hardware, and experimental validation.
- **Related map:** compare its robotics axis with CESI LINEACT’s industrial platforms; both make integration visible, but their research scopes differ.

## How to engage

1. **Watch** the medical-robotics explanation and identify the rigid and flexible parts.
2. **Read** the robotics-axis page, translating each research question into an input, computation, and physical output.
3. **Explore** PRETIL and the public laboratory directory; approach a relevant team with a small demo and a specific question, not an assumed partnership.

lessons.name: DFKI Robotics Innovation Center
lessons.summary: DFKI’s Robotics Innovation Center in Bremen develops intelligent robots for difficult environments, from underwater infrastructure to planetary exploration.
lessons.lesson_md:
## In one sentence

DFKI’s Robotics Innovation Center in Bremen develops intelligent robots for difficult environments, from underwater infrastructure to planetary exploration.

![DFKI SpaceClimber research robot](/img/lessons/orgs_research_lab_1-dfki-ric.webp)
*DFKI SpaceClimber research robot. Source: [Publisher](https://robotik.dfki-bremen.de/en/research/fields-of-application), license unknown.*

## What they do in robotics

- **Applied research:** the center combines artificial intelligence, mechanical design, electronics, and software to build working robotic systems.
- **Different environments:** its application areas include space, underwater work, logistics, production, search and rescue, and assistance.
- **Concrete example:** the Maritime Exploration Hall includes a 23 × 19 × 8-metre saltwater basin for testing robots and offshore scenarios.
- **Software analogy:** such a test facility is an integration-test environment; it exposes failures that individual algorithms or simulated unit tests can miss.

> **Key idea:** A convincing robotics result needs an environment that tests the complete system, not just a benchmark for one algorithm.

## Why they matter for 42AI

- **For 42AI:** its public demonstrations help distinguish navigation, manipulation, and whole-system reliability in demanding physical conditions.
- **Related map:** compare DFKI’s application areas with DLR Institute of Robotics and Mechatronics, another German research organization with broad robotics systems work.

## How to engage

1. **Watch** the center’s anniversary film and choose one robot application.
2. **Read** that application’s research objectives; identify what the robot must sense and which actions it must perform.
3. **Explore** the linked projects, publications, and software pages before proposing a reproducible student experiment through the published contact channel.
